question: Explain why Earth has seasons. Is it because we are closer to the Sun in summer?
answer: No. Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's rotation axis, about 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of its orbit. As Earth goes around the Sun, each hemisphere spends part of the year tilted toward the Sun: sunlight then hits it more directly, delivering more energy per square metre, and days are longer, which gives summer. Half a year later the same hemisphere is tilted away, the light comes in at a lower angle and days are shorter, which gives winter. That is why the Northern and Southern Hemispheres always have opposite seasons. Distance is not the cause: Earth is actually closest to the Sun (perihelion) in early January, during northern winter.

Distance is not the cause: perihelion (closest approach) is in early January, during northern winter
Penalize: saying seasons happen because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer, or that the orbit's ellipticity is the main cause

question: Give me the big picture on the Silk Road: what it was, when it operated, and what travelled along it besides silk.
answer: The Silk Road was not a single road but a network of trade routes linking East Asia with Central, South, Southeast and West Asia, East Africa and southern Europe; its overland routes spanned more than 6,400 km. It took shape after Han dynasty China pushed into Central Asia in the 2nd century BCE (around 114 BCE) and stayed in use until the mid-15th century, when the Ottoman Empire's control of the land routes after 1453 helped push Europeans toward sea routes. Silk, tea, porcelain, dyes, perfumes, paper, gunpowder, horses and gold moved along it, and so did ideas and religions: Buddhism spread into China along these routes, and Christianity and scientific and philosophical knowledge also travelled. It matters because it connected distant civilizations economically and culturally for some 1,500 years. The name is modern: the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen popularized 'Seidenstrasse' (Silk Road) in 1877. Parts of it are UNESCO World Heritage Sites (the Chang'an-Tianshan corridor since 2014).

Penalize: describing it as a single paved road, or attributing the name to Marco Polo or to ancient writers

question: I keep hearing that central banks raise interest rates to fight inflation. What exactly is inflation, and why would higher rates bring it down?
answer: Inflation is a rise in the average price level of goods and services, so each unit of money buys less; it is usually measured with a consumer price index (CPI) that tracks the price of a basket of typical purchases. Most major central banks, including the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of England, target low and stable inflation of about 2% a year (New Zealand pioneered formal inflation targeting in 1990). When inflation runs above target, the central bank raises its policy interest rate. Borrowing becomes more expensive (mortgages, business loans, credit cards) and saving more attractive, so households and firms borrow, spend and invest less. Lower demand eases the pressure on prices, and a credible central bank also keeps people's expectations of future inflation in check. The trade-off is that higher rates cool the whole economy and can slow growth and raise unemployment; cutting rates has the opposite effect.

Penalize: claiming higher interest rates raise inflation in the standard view, or that central banks fight inflation by printing money

question: I'm visiting Thingvellir (Þingvellir) in Iceland and the guide says I can stand between two continents. What does that actually mean geologically?
answer: Þingvellir lies in a rift valley on the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the boundary where the North American Plate and the Eurasian Plate are moving apart. Along most of its length the ridge is deep under the ocean, but in Iceland it rises above sea level, so the boundary is visible as cracks and faults running across the park. The plates separate at an average of about 2.5 cm per year along the ridge, and new crust forms from volcanic activity to fill the gap, which is why Iceland has frequent volcanism and earthquakes. So 'between two continents' really means standing in the rift between two tectonic plates, not on a line between Europe and America as landmasses. The Silfra fissure in the lake is one of these cracks and is popular for snorkelling and diving. The site also matters historically: Iceland's assembly, the Althing, met there from 930, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2004).

May add the Althing (930) and UNESCO status
Penalize: saying the plates are colliding/converging, or naming the African or Pacific plate as one of the two

question: Explain Plato's allegory of the cave and what it is meant to show.
answer: The allegory is in Plato's Republic, Book VII (514a-520a), told by Socrates to Glaucon. Prisoners have been chained all their lives facing the back wall of a cave. Behind them burns a fire, and objects carried in front of it cast shadows on the wall; the shadows and their echoes are all the prisoners know, so they take them for reality. One prisoner is freed. He is dazzled first by the fire and then by daylight outside, but gradually he learns to see real things and finally the Sun itself. The Sun stands for the Form of the Good, the source of truth and intelligibility, while the shadows stand for the world of the senses and mere opinion. If he went back down, his eyes would no longer be used to the dark; the others would conclude the journey had harmed him and would even kill anyone who tried to drag them out. Plato uses it to show the effect of education, and of its absence, on our nature: education turns the soul from appearances toward knowledge of the Forms, grasped by reason rather than the senses.

question: How does a GPS receiver in a phone or car work out where it is?
answer: Each GPS satellite carries very stable atomic clocks and continuously broadcasts its precise time and its position in orbit. The receiver only listens; it does not transmit anything and needs no phone or internet signal for GPS itself. From the moment each signal arrives, it computes how long the signal travelled and so how far away that satellite is (travel time multiplied by the speed of light). Distances to several satellites at known positions pin down a single point. It needs at least four satellites, because there are four unknowns: three position coordinates plus the error of its own inexpensive clock. The satellites orbit at about 20,200 km, and relativity matters: seen from the ground their clocks run about 38 microseconds per day fast, which the system corrects for. GPS is owned by the United States Space Force.

Penalize: claiming the phone sends signals to the satellites, or that one or two satellites are enough for a 3D fix

question: I'll be in Oaxaca, Mexico, at the start of November and people say I'll see Day of the Dead celebrations. What is the holiday about? Is it just Mexican Halloween?
answer: Day of the Dead (Dia de Muertos) is a Mexican tradition, held mainly on 1 and 2 November, in which families honour and remember relatives who have died and welcome their souls back for a visit. Families build ofrendas, altars at home or at the grave, with photos, candles and the dead person's favourite foods and drinks, and they decorate graves. Orange cempasuchil marigolds are used because they are believed to attract the souls and guide them from the cemetery to the family home. Sugar or clay calaveras (skulls), often inscribed with a name, are given as gifts, and La Catrina, the elegantly dressed female skeleton created by the printmaker Jose Guadalupe Posada, is its best-known image. It is not Mexican Halloween: both fall around 31 October to 2 November (Allhallowtide), but Day of the Dead is about remembering loved ones in a warm, festive way rather than about fright or costumes. UNESCO inscribed it on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008.

Purpose: honouring and remembering deceased relatives, whose souls are welcomed back

question: Describe what causes ocean tides and why some tides are much bigger than others.
answer: Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity, with a smaller contribution from the Sun. What matters is the difference in pull across Earth (the tidal force): the ocean on the side facing the Moon is pulled a little more than Earth's centre, and the far side a little less, so the water forms two bulges. As Earth rotates through them, most coasts get two high and two low tides a day, with high tides about 12 hours 25 minutes apart, because the Moon returns to the same place in the sky every 24 hours 50 minutes. The Sun's tidal effect is about 46% of the Moon's. When the Sun, Moon and Earth line up, at new and full moon, their effects add and produce spring tides with the largest range (the name has nothing to do with the season). When the Sun and Moon are at right angles, at first and third quarter, they partly cancel and produce neap tides with the smallest range. Coastline shape matters too: funnel-shaped bays amplify tides, and the Bay of Fundy in Canada has ranges of over 16 metres.

question: How did the Meiji Restoration transform Japan, and what did it overturn?
answer: The Meiji Restoration was the political revolution of 1868 that returned power to the imperial house under Emperor Meiji and ended the Tokugawa shogunate. On 3 January 1868 the restoration of imperial rule was proclaimed, and the Boshin War of 1868-1869 defeated the shogunate's remaining supporters. Edo was renamed Tokyo ('eastern capital') in 1868, and the capital moved there from Kyoto. The new government then rebuilt Japan along modern, largely Western lines: the Charter Oath of 1868 set out its aims; the feudal domains were abolished and power centralized; the samurai class was eliminated; the army and administration were modernized; industry and Western technology were adopted; and the Meiji Constitution of 1889 created the framework of imperial government until after the Second World War. Within a few decades Japan went from an isolated feudal society to a modern industrial and imperial power.

question: Summarize how Gutenberg's printing press changed Europe, and whether he was the first to print with movable type.
answer: Around 1440 in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined a screw press, movable metal type cast from a lead-tin-antimony alloy, and an oil-based ink into a practical system for printing books; his Bible was finished around 1454-1455. Printing spread remarkably fast: by 1500 presses were working in about 270 European cities and had produced more than 20 million copies. Books and pamphlets became far cheaper and more plentiful, which spread literacy, information and new ideas. It gave the Protestant Reformation enormous reach: Martin Luther became Europe's most published author, with about 300,000 copies of his works printed between 1518 and 1520. Gutenberg was not the first to print with movable type: Bi Sheng invented movable type made of baked clay in 11th-century China, and the Korean Jikji (1377) is the oldest surviving book printed with metal movable type. What Gutenberg created was a system efficient enough for mass production, which those earlier methods never achieved in their regions.

question: If the Sun suddenly vanished, how long would it take before we on Earth noticed, both in light and in gravity?
answer: About 8 minutes 19 seconds for both. Earth is on average one astronomical unit from the Sun, about 149.6 million km, and light covers that in roughly 499 seconds. Changes in gravity also travel at the speed of light: in 2017 the gravitational waves and the light from the neutron-star merger GW170817 arrived only 1.7 seconds apart, confirming they travel at essentially the same speed. So for about 8 minutes Earth would keep curving around the now-empty point as if nothing had happened; then, at the same moment the sky went dark, it would start moving off in a straight line. (A Sun cannot really vanish, since mass-energy is conserved, so this is a thought experiment.)

question: I'm flying from Tokyo to Honolulu, leaving Monday at 9 pm local time, and the flight takes about 7 hours. What day and time will it be in Honolulu when I land, and why?
answer: You land around 9 am on the same Monday, so by the clock you arrive about 12 hours 'before' you left. Japan Standard Time is UTC+9 and Hawaii is UTC-10, and neither observes daylight saving time, so Honolulu clocks are 19 hours behind Tokyo. Departure at 21:00 Monday in Tokyo is 12:00 UTC Monday; seven hours later it is 19:00 UTC Monday, which is 09:00 Monday in Honolulu. The reason is the International Date Line: flying east across it sets the date back by one day, which more than cancels the hours you gain crossing time zones eastward.

question: I'm staying in La Paz, Bolivia, and my pasta takes much longer to cook than at home by the sea. Why, and roughly what temperature does water boil at here?
answer: Because of the altitude. La Paz sits at roughly 3,650 m, and the lower air pressure up there lowers the boiling point of water. The boiling point drops by roughly 1 degree C for every 275-300 m of climb (about 1 degree F per 500 ft): it is about 96-97 degrees C at 1,500 m and about 90-91 degrees C at 3,000 m, so in La Paz water boils at roughly 87-89 degrees C instead of 100 degrees C. Since boiling water cannot get hotter than its boiling point, food cooks more slowly; turning up the stove just makes it boil harder, not hotter. Cook longer, keep a lid on, or use a pressure cooker, which raises the pressure and so brings the boiling temperature back toward 100 degrees C.

question: Work out how many people you need in a room for a better-than-even chance that two of them share a birthday, and explain why the number is so small.
answer: 23 people. Assuming 365 equally likely birthdays (ignoring 29 February and twins), the chance that all 23 birthdays are different is (365/365) x (364/365) x ... x (343/365), about 0.493, so the chance that at least two match is about 50.7%. The number is small because what matters is pairs of people, not people: 23 people form 23 x 22 / 2 = 253 pairs, and each pair is a separate chance of a match. The probability climbs quickly; with 70 people it is about 99.9%. Note that this is the chance that any two people share any birthday; the chance that someone shares your own birthday is much lower.

question: If I put money in an account paying 6% a year, compounded annually, and never withdraw, about how long until it doubles? Is there a quick rule of thumb?
answer: About 12 years. The rule of 72 says the doubling time is roughly 72 divided by the annual interest rate in percent, so 72 / 6 = 12 years. The exact figure is ln(2) / ln(1.06), about 11.9 years (1.06 to the 12th power is about 2.01). The rule works best for rates of roughly 6-10%; for lower rates, 70 or 69.3 gives slightly better estimates. It ignores taxes, fees and inflation, so in real terms your purchasing power doubles more slowly. Without compounding (simple interest) it would take about 16.7 years.

question: Is Rome farther north than New York City? And if so, why are Rome's winters milder?
answer: Yes, slightly. Rome is at about 41.9 degrees N and New York City at about 40.7 degrees N, so Rome is roughly 1.2 degrees of latitude, about 130 km, farther north. Yet Rome has a Mediterranean climate with mild winters (January averages about 7.5 degrees C), while New York has a humid subtropical climate with cold winters (January lows around -2 degrees C, highs around 4 degrees C). Latitude alone does not set climate: much of Europe is warmer than places at the same latitude elsewhere, partly because of the North Atlantic Current (the extension of the Gulf Stream) bringing warm water toward Europe, and Rome also sits beside the Mediterranean Sea, whereas New York's winters are shaped by the North American continent.

question: Explain whether you should switch doors in the Monty Hall problem, and why the answer isn't 50/50.
answer: Switch: under the standard rules switching wins the car 2/3 of the time and staying wins only 1/3. The standard rules are that the host knows where the car is, always opens one of the two unchosen doors to show a goat, and always offers the switch. Your first pick is right only 1/3 of the time, and nothing the host does changes that. In the other 2/3 of cases you picked a goat; the host must then open the other goat door, so the remaining closed door has the car. Switching therefore wins exactly when your first pick was wrong, which is 2/3 of the time. It is not 50/50 because the host's choice is not random; it gives you information. If the host did not know and happened to open a goat door at random, switching would win only half the time. The puzzle became famous after Marilyn vos Savant's 1990 Parade column, when thousands of readers wrongly insisted she was mistaken.

question: Why was 1900 not a leap year when 2000 was?
answer: Because of the Gregorian calendar rule: a year divisible by 4 is a leap year, except years divisible by 100, which are leap years only if they are also divisible by 400. 1900 is divisible by 100 but not by 400, so it was an ordinary year; 2000 is divisible by 400, so it was a leap year (as was 1600, while 1700, 1800 and 2100 are not). The reason is accuracy. The tropical (solar) year is about 365.2422 days. The older Julian calendar added a leap day every 4 years, giving an average year of 365.25 days, which slowly drifted against the seasons. Dropping three leap days every 400 years gives an average of 365.2425 days, very close to the real year. Pope Gregory XIII introduced the reform in 1582, skipping 10 days: Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October.

question: I saw a lightning flash and counted 9 seconds before the thunder. How far away was the strike, and am I safe at that distance?
answer: About 3 km, just under 2 miles. The light arrives essentially instantly, while sound travels at about 343 m/s in air at 20 degrees C, so 9 s x 343 m/s is about 3,100 m. Rules of thumb: divide the seconds by 3 for kilometres, or by 5 for miles (9 / 5 = about 1.8 miles). You are not safe at that distance: if you can hear thunder, you are likely within striking distance of the storm, and thunder is only audible up to about 10 miles (16 km) from a strike. Go indoors into a substantial building or a hard-topped vehicle, and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back outside.

question: Check this claim: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
answer: True. The Great Pyramid was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2600 BC. Cleopatra VII died in 30 BC, roughly 2,570 years later. The Apollo 11 Moon landing was on 20 July 1969, about 2,000 years after her death (30 BC to AD 1969 is 1,998 years, because there is no year zero). So she lived roughly 500 years closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramid's construction; to her, the Great Pyramid was already very ancient.

question: How does a virus differ from a bacterium, and why won't antibiotics help with a cold?
answer: Bacteria are single-celled living organisms, prokaryotes without a nucleus, typically about 0.5-5 micrometres long. They have their own metabolism and reproduce on their own by dividing (binary fission). Most are harmless or beneficial, such as the many bacteria in our gut; only some cause disease, such as tuberculosis or cholera. Viruses are much smaller, typically 20-300 nanometres, and are not cells: they have no metabolism of their own and can replicate only inside the living cells of a host, using its machinery. Antibiotics act on bacteria, so they only work against bacterial infections. Colds are caused by viruses, so antibiotics do not relieve the symptoms or speed recovery; a cold usually gets better on its own in 1-2 weeks. Some viral infections can be treated with antiviral drugs or prevented with vaccines. Unnecessary antibiotic use also drives antibiotic resistance.

question: Compare Sunni and Shia Islam: how did the split begin, and how large is each branch?
answer: The split began as a dispute over who should lead the Muslim community after the Prophet Muhammad died in 632 CE. Those who became Sunnis held that Muhammad had not appointed a successor and accepted Abu Bakr, chosen by the community, as the first caliph. Those who became Shia (from shi'at Ali, 'the followers of Ali') believed Muhammad had designated Ali, his cousin and son-in-law, and that leadership belonged to Muhammad's family line through the Imams. The division deepened after Ali's son Husayn was killed at Karbala in 680, which Shia Muslims commemorate on Ashura. Both branches share the Quran and the five pillars of Islam; they differ mainly on religious authority (the Shia doctrine of the Imamate), some practices and law. Sunnis are the large majority, about 85% of Muslims (roughly 1.7-1.8 billion people); Shia are about 15% (roughly 285-300 million). Shia form majorities in Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan and Bahrain and large communities in Lebanon and elsewhere.

question: Compare nuclear fission and nuclear fusion: how each works, where each is used today, and which one powers the Sun.
answer: Fission splits a heavy nucleus, usually uranium-235 or plutonium-239, into smaller nuclei, releasing energy and extra neutrons that can trigger further fissions in a chain reaction. It was discovered in 1938 by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann and explained by Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch in 1939. Fission is what all of today's nuclear power plants use (several hundred reactors worldwide) and what powered the first nuclear weapons; its drawbacks include radioactive waste and the need to control the chain reaction. Fusion joins light nuclei, such as the hydrogen isotopes deuterium and tritium, into a heavier nucleus such as helium, releasing energy. Fusion powers the Sun and other stars: the Sun's core fuses about 620 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second. On Earth, controlled fusion is still experimental: in December 2022 the US National Ignition Facility for the first time produced more fusion energy (3.15 MJ) than the laser energy delivered to the target (2.05 MJ), but no commercial fusion power plant is operating.

question: Is Mount Everest really the tallest mountain on Earth, or do Mauna Kea and Chimborazo have a claim?
answer: It depends on how you measure. Everest has the highest summit above sea level, 8,848.86 m. Mauna Kea in Hawaii rises only 4,207 m above sea level, but most of the volcano is under the ocean; measured from its base on the sea floor it is roughly 9,300-10,200 m tall (figures vary because the base is loosely defined), more than Everest's height above sea level, so it is often called the tallest mountain from base to peak. Chimborazo in Ecuador (6,263 m) has the summit farthest from Earth's centre, about 6,384.4 km, roughly 2 km farther than Everest's, because it lies just south of the equator where Earth's equatorial bulge is greatest. So: highest elevation above sea level, Everest; tallest from base to summit, Mauna Kea; farthest from Earth's centre, Chimborazo.

Chimborazo: summit farthest from Earth's centre (~2 km farther than Everest) because of the equatorial bulge
Clear verdict that the answer depends on the definition
Penalize: saying Mauna Kea or Chimborazo is higher than Everest above sea level

question: I'm walking around the Roman Forum and the guide keeps switching between 'the Republic' and 'the Empire'. What's the difference, and when did one become the other?
answer: They are two phases of Roman government. The Republic began, by tradition, in 509 BC when the Romans overthrew their last king, Tarquin the Proud. Power was shared: two consuls, elected for one year and each able to veto the other, led the state together with the Senate and popular assemblies. In the 1st century BC the Republic broke down in civil wars between powerful generals, first Marius and Sulla, then Julius Caesar and Pompey. Caesar was assassinated in 44 BC; his heir Octavian won the civil wars that followed, and in 27 BC the Senate gave him the title Augustus. That is the conventional start of the Empire: the Senate still existed, but real power, above all control of the army, lay with one ruler, the emperor (princeps). Julius Caesar himself was never emperor. Rome already ruled a large territorial empire under the Republic; the terms refer to the system of government. The Western Empire ended in 476 AD and the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire in 1453.

May add end dates: West 476 AD, East 1453
Penalize: saying Julius Caesar was the first emperor, or dating the start of the Empire to 44 BC or 476 AD

question: My friend asked me to lie to protect her, and I can't decide if that's OK. How would Kant and John Stuart Mill each look at lying in that situation?
answer: They reason in opposite ways. Kant judges an act by its principle, not its outcome: you should act only on a maxim you could will as a universal law, and treat people always as ends, never merely as means (the categorical imperative, in the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785). Lying fails that test, since if everyone lied when it suited them, trust in what people say would collapse. Kant held the duty of truthfulness to be so strict that, replying to Benjamin Constant in a 1797 essay, he argued you may not lie even to a murderer at your door who asks where your friend is hiding, although you may refuse to answer. Mill is a utilitarian: an act is right insofar as it promotes the greatest happiness of everyone affected (Utilitarianism, 1861/1863), so consequences decide. He treated truthfulness as a very important rule of thumb, because trust is so valuable, but a lie that prevents serious harm can be justified when the outcome is clearly better. So for Kant the answer is no, even to protect your friend; for Mill it depends on what harm the lie prevents and how much it damages trust.

question: What is the Bitcoin halving, how often does it happen, and how does it relate to the 21 million cap?
answer: The halving is the built-in rule that cuts the block subsidy, the new bitcoins a miner earns for each block, in half every 210,000 blocks. With blocks found about every 10 minutes on average, that is roughly every four years. The subsidy started at 50 BTC per block when the network launched (genesis block, 3 January 2009) and has fallen to 25, 12.5, 6.25 and, after the April 2024 halving, 3.125 BTC. Because each 210,000-block era issues half as many coins as the one before, total issuance is a geometric series that converges to just under 21 million BTC (50 x 210,000 x 2 = 21 million); the last fractions should be issued around the year 2140. After that, miners would be paid only through transaction fees. Halvings are triggered by block height, not by the calendar, so the four-year rhythm is approximate.

question: Explain the difference between proof of work and proof of stake, using Ethereum's switch in 2022 as the example.
answer: Both are ways for a blockchain's nodes to agree on which blocks are valid and in what order, while making attacks expensive. In proof of work, miners compete to solve a hash puzzle by brute-force computation; the winner adds the next block and earns the reward, and rewriting history would require out-computing the rest of the network, which costs hardware and electricity. In proof of stake, validators lock up the chain's own coin as collateral (on Ethereum, a deposit of 32 ETH per validator) and are randomly chosen to propose blocks while committees attest to them. Misbehaviour such as proposing two blocks for the same slot or making contradictory attestations is punished by slashing part or all of the stake, and reverting finalized blocks would require burning at least a third of all staked ETH. Ethereum switched in the Merge on 15 September 2022, when its original proof-of-work chain merged with the Beacon Chain, a proof-of-stake chain running since 1 December 2020. Mining ended and energy use fell by about 99.95%. The Merge was a change of consensus mechanism, not a capacity upgrade, so it was not meant to lower gas fees.

PoS: validators stake coins (32 ETH on Ethereum), propose/attest; slashing punishes misbehaviour; finality

question: My phone wallet app still opens, but I lost the paper with my 12-word recovery phrase. What should I do?
answer: Act now while you still have access. The recovery (seed) phrase is the master backup: it can regenerate all your private keys and restore the wallet on any device, and anyone who finds it can take your funds. Since you can't be sure nobody found the paper, the safe course is: (1) create a new wallet with a fresh recovery phrase; write the new phrase down on paper and store it securely offline, never as a screenshot, photo, cloud note or email; (2) transfer all your funds and tokens from the old wallet to the new one; (3) stop using the old wallet. Some apps let you view the old phrase again after entering your PIN, but if it may have been exposed, moving the funds is still the right move. Never share your phrase or type it into a website or chat, including for anyone claiming to be support: no legitimate service will ask for it. If your phone breaks before you do this, the funds are likely lost for good, because without the phrase nobody can restore the wallet.

question: Fees on Ethereum mainnet are too high for my small payments, and someone suggested using a rollup like Arbitrum or Optimism. What is a rollup, and what's the catch?
answer: A rollup is a layer-2 network that executes transactions off Ethereum's main chain, bundles ('rolls up') many of them into batches, and posts the compressed transaction data plus a commitment to the result back to Ethereum as calldata or blobs. Because the layer-1 cost is shared across many transactions, fees are much lower, while Ethereum still guarantees the data and, through proofs, the correctness of the result. There are two main types. Optimistic rollups, such as Arbitrum and Optimism, assume batches are valid and rely on fraud proofs: anyone can challenge an invalid batch during a challenge period of about seven days, so a direct withdrawal back to Ethereum mainnet takes about a week; third-party liquidity providers can pay you out sooner for a fee. ZK (zero-knowledge) rollups instead post a validity proof that Ethereum verifies, so there is no challenge period and withdrawals can be fast, but generating the proofs is expensive and complex. The catches: the withdrawal delay on optimistic rollups, extra smart-contract and bridge risk, and the fact that rollups often rely on a single sequencer to order transactions.

ZK rollups: validity proofs, no challenge period, faster withdrawals, but costly/complex proving

Penalize: claiming optimistic rollups allow instant native withdrawals, or that rollups have security independent of Ethereum

question: What can an attacker actually do with a 51% attack on a proof-of-work blockchain, and what can't they do?
answer: With more than half of the network's hash power, an attacker can mine a private chain faster than everyone else and then publish it, causing a reorganization that replaces recent blocks. That lets them double-spend, for example by depositing coins at an exchange, withdrawing something else, and then rewriting history so the deposit never happened. They can also censor transactions and stop other miners' blocks from staying in the chain. What they cannot do is steal coins from other people's addresses, forge signatures, or create coins beyond the protocol's rules: honest nodes reject invalid transactions and blocks, so, as the Bitcoin whitepaper puts it, an attacker can only try to change one of his own transactions to take back money he recently spent. Large networks are very expensive to attack this way, but smaller proof-of-work coins have been hit: Ethereum Classic suffered several 51% attacks in 2019-2020, and Bitcoin Gold lost about $18 million to double-spends in 2018. Waiting for more confirmations on large payments reduces the risk.

Cannot: steal others' coins, forge signatures, mint coins beyond the rules (nodes reject invalid transactions)
Real examples: Ethereum Classic (2019-2020), Bitcoin Gold (2018)
Mitigation: more confirmations; cost of attack scales with hash power
Penalize: claiming a 51% attacker can take coins from any address or print unlimited new coins

question: Explain what 'gas' is on Ethereum and what the EIP-1559 fee change did.
answer: Gas is the unit that measures the computational effort an Ethereum operation requires; a plain ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas. You pay the gas used times a price per unit of gas, usually quoted in gwei (one billionth of an ETH). EIP-1559, activated in the London upgrade on 5 August 2021, replaced the old first-price auction, where users simply bid gas prices, with a two-part fee. The base fee is set by the protocol: it rises or falls by up to 12.5% per block depending on whether the previous block used more or less than the target, which is half the block gas limit (blocks can stretch to twice the target), and it is burned, removed from circulation rather than paid to anyone. The priority fee (tip) goes to the block producer, which has meant validators since the Merge. Users set a maximum fee and are refunded the difference between it and base fee plus tip. The main effect was to make fees more predictable; it did not make them cheap, since fees still rise with demand.

question: Explain what a Merkle tree is and why Bitcoin puts a Merkle root in each block header.
answer: A Merkle tree, or hash tree (patented by Ralph Merkle in 1979), is built by hashing each data item, in Bitcoin each transaction, and then repeatedly hashing pairs of hashes together until a single hash is left: the Merkle root. Changing any transaction changes the root. Bitcoin puts only this root in the block header, so the small header commits to every transaction in the block. The Bitcoin whitepaper uses this in two ways. First, old spent transactions can be pruned to save disk space without breaking the block's hash. Second, Simplified Payment Verification (SPV): a light wallet keeps only the chain of block headers and checks that a transaction is included by obtaining the Merkle branch, the short list of hashes linking the transaction to the root. The proof size grows only with the logarithm of the number of transactions, about 12 hashes for a block of 4,000 transactions, instead of downloading the whole block.

Penalize: saying the Merkle root stores the full transactions, or that Satoshi invented Merkle trees

question: Napoleon was famously very short. How tall was he exactly, and did his height drive his ambition?
answer: The premise is a myth: Napoleon was not unusually short. He is estimated at about 1.67-1.70 m (roughly 5 ft 6-7 in), close to the average height of men of his time. The myth has two main sources. His height was recorded as 5 pieds 2 pouces in old French units, about 1.68 m, which English readers took as 5 ft 2 in because the French inch was longer than the English one. And British caricaturists, notably James Gillray, kept drawing him as tiny to mock him. An exact figure cannot be given, since sources differ slightly. The 'Napoleon complex', the idea that short men compensate with aggression or ambition, is named after this myth, and the research on it is mixed: some studies found no such effect, others a small one. There is no evidence that height drove his ambition.

question: Tell me who Jack the Ripper really was.
answer: His identity is unknown. 'Jack the Ripper' is the name given to an unidentified serial killer active in and around the Whitechapel district of London in 1888. question: I'm reading a novel set in Brazil in the 1950s. Which city was the country's capital at that time?
answer: Rio de Janeiro. Rio was Brazil's capital from 1763 until 21 April 1960, when the newly built Brasilia, planned by Lucio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer under President Juscelino Kubitschek, was inaugurated as the capital. So throughout the 1950s the capital was Rio. Before 1763, Salvador, in Bahia, had been the colonial capital. Sao Paulo has never been the national capital.

question: Do you really need to drink eight glasses of water a day?
answer: Not as a strict rule. The common advice to drink 8 glasses of plain water a day has no firm scientific basis, and needs vary with body size, activity, climate and health; for most healthy people thirst is a better guide than a fixed amount. The NHS suggests about 6 to 8 cups or glasses of fluid a day, and that fluid includes not only water but also lower-fat milk and lower-sugar drinks, including tea and coffee. Food also supplies a meaningful share of total water, roughly 20%. The European Food Safety Authority's reference intakes are about 2.0 litres a day for women and 2.5 litres for men of total water from drinks and food. A practical check from the NHS is to drink enough that your pee is a pale colour; dark yellow, strong-smelling pee, thirst and headache are signs of dehydration. You need more when it is hot, during long or hard exercise, when you are ill, and when pregnant or breastfeeding. People with a medical condition who have been told to limit fluids should follow their doctor's advice.

question: I have a 12-hour flight next week. How do I lower my risk of a blood clot in my legs, and what symptoms would be a warning sign?
answer: For most healthy travellers the risk is small, but any journey longer than about 4 hours raises it. To lower it: get up and walk around the cabin every 1-2 hours when it is safe to do so; while seated, exercise your calf muscles by extending your legs and flexing your ankles; wear loose, comfortable clothing; drink enough water and avoid alcohol. If you have extra risk factors, such as a previous blood clot, recent surgery or hospital stay, pregnancy, hormonal contraception, obesity, older age or limited mobility, talk to a doctor before the trip; they may recommend graduated compression stockings or other measures. Warning signs of a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), during or after the trip, are swelling, throbbing or cramping pain or tenderness, warm skin and red or darkened skin, usually in one leg; get medical advice promptly. Shortness of breath, chest pain, a fast or irregular heartbeat, coughing up blood or fainting can mean a clot has travelled to the lungs (pulmonary embolism): call emergency services immediately.

question: Give me practical advice for beating jet lag after a flight east across six time zones.
answer: Expect several days of adjustment: on average the body clock re-adjusts by about one day per time zone crossed, so six zones can take up to around six days. Eastward trips are usually harder, because the body clock runs slightly longer than 24 hours and is easier to delay than to advance. Before you go, start shifting your sleep toward destination time (for an eastward trip, earlier to bed and earlier up). On the plane, drink plenty of water, avoid too much caffeine and alcohol, walk and stretch, and try to sleep if it is night-time at your destination. After arrival, switch to local time straight away: sleep and eat on the local schedule, avoid daytime naps, and set an alarm so you don't oversleep. Get outside in daylight, since light is the strongest signal for resetting the body clock. Melatonin is used by some travellers and some studies suggest it helps, but the NHS does not recommend it for jet lag because the evidence is insufficient; sleeping pills may help briefly with severe insomnia but can be addictive.

question: What does SPF on sunscreen mean, and is SPF 50 much better than SPF 30?
answer: SPF (sun protection factor) measures protection against UVB, the rays that mainly cause sunburn. Applied at the test amount of 2 mg per square centimetre of skin, SPF 15 lets through about 1/15 of the burning UVB and blocks about 93%, SPF 30 blocks about 97% and SPF 50 about 98%. So on paper SPF 50 is only slightly better than SPF 30. In practice people apply only a quarter to half of the test amount, which cuts real protection a lot, so applying enough and reapplying matter more than the number. SPF says nothing about UVA: look for 'broad spectrum' or, in the UK, a UVA star rating of at least 4 stars. The NHS advises at least SPF 30 with 4-star UVA protection, applied generously and reapplied every 2 hours and after swimming, sweating or towel-drying, together with shade (in the UK between 11am and 3pm from March to October), clothing, a hat and sunglasses; sunscreen alone is not enough.

question: I'm on a beach in Chile and just felt a strong earthquake that went on for a long time. The shaking has stopped. What should I do now?
answer: Treat the shaking itself as your tsunami warning and get to high ground now; do not wait for an official alert or siren. Move immediately, on foot if you can, as high and as far inland as possible: aim for ground at least 30 m (100 ft) above sea level or at least 1.5 km (1 mile) inland, following tsunami evacuation signs if there are any. Do not go to the shore to look. If the sea suddenly drains away exposing the seabed, or rises suddenly, or you hear a roar from the ocean, a wave is coming. If there are aftershocks, drop, cover your head and neck and hold on until the shaking stops, then keep moving. A tsunami is a series of waves, so stay on high ground and away from the coast until local authorities say it is safe to return. If you are caught in the water, grab onto something that floats. Context matters: indoors away from the coast, the advice during shaking is to drop, cover and hold on and stay inside; on the coast, strong or long shaking means evacuate inland as soon as it stops.

question: Tell me what to do if a strong earthquake starts while I'm inside a building, including if I'm in bed.
answer: Drop, Cover, and Hold On, and stay inside. Drop where you are onto your hands and knees. Cover your head and neck with one arm and hand, and if a sturdy table or desk is nearby, crawl underneath it. Hold on until the shaking stops, keeping one hand on your shelter and being ready to move with it if it shifts. If you are in bed, stay there: turn face down and cover your head and neck with a pillow. Do not run outside while the ground is shaking, and avoid doorways. If you use a wheelchair, lock the wheels, bend over and cover your head and neck with your arms, a book or a pillow, and hold on. Afterwards, expect aftershocks and drop, cover and hold on again if one comes. Context changes the advice: if you are outdoors, move to an open area away from buildings, trees, streetlights and power lines; if you are driving, pull over, stop and set the parking brake; and if you are in a coastal area that may get tsunamis, go inland or to higher ground as soon as the shaking stops.

question: I'm hiking in hot weather and my friend is dizzy, has a headache, feels sick and is sweating a lot. What should I do, and when does it become an emergency?
answer: These are signs of heat exhaustion, which does not usually need emergency help if the person can cool down within 30 minutes. Act now: move them to a cool, shaded place; remove unnecessary clothing such as a jacket or socks; give them plenty of water or an isotonic sports drink; and cool their skin by spraying or sponging them with cool water and fanning them. Cold packs wrapped in cloth under the armpits or on the neck also help. Stay with them; they should start to cool down and feel better within 30 minutes. It becomes an emergency, so call emergency services (999 in the UK, 911 in the US), if they are still unwell after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place and cooling, or if they show signs of heatstroke: a very high temperature, hot skin that is no longer sweating, a fast heartbeat or fast breathing, confusion or lack of coordination, a seizure or fit, or loss of consciousness. Keep cooling them while you wait for help, and if they lose consciousness, put them in the recovery position.

Keep cooling while waiting; recovery position if unconscious
Penalize: advising to keep hiking to 'walk it off', giving alcohol, or waiting hours before calling for help when heatstroke signs appear

question: I'm on an exposed ridge above the treeline, a thunderstorm is rolling in, and the nearest building is an hour's walk away. How do I stay safe?
answer: No place outdoors is safe during a thunderstorm, so the aim is to cut your risk while you head for real shelter. Get off the ridge immediately: descend from peaks, ridges and other high points toward lower ground. Do not shelter under an isolated tree, get away from ponds, lakes and other water, and stay away from things that conduct electricity, such as wire fences and power lines. Never lie flat on the ground. If you are in a group, spread out so that one strike cannot injure everyone. Keep moving toward a substantial building or a hard-topped vehicle, the only truly safe shelters, and do not resume your hike until at least 30 minutes after the last thunder. Context matters: with a building or car nearby, the right move is simply to get inside at the first thunder ('when thunder roars, go indoors'); on an exposed ridge with no shelter close, losing height quickly is the most important step.

question: What should you do if a carbon monoxide alarm goes off at home and people are feeling headachy and dizzy?
answer: Treat it as carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone out into fresh air immediately. If you can do it on the way out without delay, switch off fuel-burning appliances such as a boiler, heater or cooker. Do not go back inside until the source has been checked and you have been told it is safe. Call emergency services (911 in the US, 999 in the UK) if anyone has difficulty breathing, is confused, very drowsy, has chest pain or loses consciousness; otherwise get medical advice promptly (in the UK, NHS 111) and say you suspect carbon monoxide. Report the suspected appliance or gas fault (in the UK, the National Gas Helpline 0800 111 999). Headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea or vomiting, chest pain and confusion are typical, flu-like CO symptoms, and they often improve once you are outside, which is another clue. CO is an odourless, colourless gas, and people who are asleep or drunk can die from it before they have symptoms, so never silence the alarm and stay inside.

question: Why did the Western Roman Empire fall?
answer: There was no single cause; historians weigh many interacting factors, and some prefer to describe a gradual transformation into post-Roman kingdoms rather than a sudden fall. The conventional end date is 476, when the Germanic leader Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus. Commonly cited factors: (1) political instability, with repeated civil wars and succession struggles that weakened the state and diverted armies; (2) pressure from migrating and invading peoples, especially Goths fleeing the Huns, then Vandals and others, including the sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410 and by the Vandals in 455; (3) fiscal and military strain: losing tax-rich provinces, above all North Africa and Carthage to the Vandals in 439, meant less money to pay armies, which made further losses more likely, while heavy military spending and taxation weighed on the economy; (4) the division of the empire after 395, which left the West to face its threats largely on its own; and, in some accounts, epidemics, climate deterioration, inequality and corruption. The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire survived until 1453.

Penalize: a single-cause answer presented as settled, or dating the Western fall to 1453 or 410

question: Explain the Black Death: what caused it, how deadly it was, and how it changed European society afterward.
answer: The Black Death was a plague pandemic that struck Eurasia and North Africa from 1346 to 1353; it reached Europe in 1347, reportedly via Genoese traders from Kaffa in Crimea, arriving in Sicily that October. It was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, spread mainly by the bites of fleas carried by rats (bubonic plague) and also directly between people in its pneumonic form. It killed an estimated 25-50 million people in Europe, around 30-60% of the population, and possibly 75-200 million across Eurasia and North Africa; Europe's population did not return to its earlier level until the 16th century, and plague kept recurring for centuries. Consequences: the severe labour shortage pushed wages up and rents down, and surviving commoners inherited property and gained mobility, which weakened the feudal order, though inflation ate into many workers' real incomes. Religious fervour surged, including flagellant movements, along with violent scapegoating: Jews were accused of poisoning wells, and by 1351 some 60 major and 150 smaller Jewish communities had been destroyed. Public-health responses also emerged, notably quarantine, from Ragusa's 40-day isolation rule of 1377.

question: I'm visiting Manchester, which is often called the first industrial city. Why did the Industrial Revolution start in Britain, and what did it change?
answer: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain around 1760 and ran to roughly 1820-1840, then spread to continental Europe and the United States. Britain went first because of a combination of factors: plentiful coal and iron, plus water power; a productive agriculture (the British Agricultural Revolution) that freed labour and produced food surpluses; political stability, a legal system favourable to business, and access to capital; ports, rivers and canals for transport; trade and colonial plantations supplying raw cotton; and relatively high wages alongside cheap energy, which made labour-saving machines worth building. Its core changes were textile machines such as the spinning jenny, water frame and power loom, factories, James Watt's improved steam engines, and coke-smelted iron; mechanized cotton spinning raised output per worker roughly 500-fold. Manchester, nicknamed 'Cottonopolis', grew around cotton mills and became the world's first industrialized city; the Bridgewater Canal (1761) brought in coal, and the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (1830) was the world's first intercity passenger railway. Socially it brought rapid urbanization and population growth, factory labour including child labour, and pollution, and over the long run unprecedented sustained growth in average income, although historians debate how quickly living standards rose for ordinary workers.

question: I'm taking my UK hair dryer and laptop charger to Japan. Will they work there, and what do I need?
answer: The plugs won't fit, and the hair dryer probably won't work properly. Japan uses 100 V mains, at 50 Hz in eastern Japan (including Tokyo) and 60 Hz in western Japan (including Osaka), with Type A sockets (two flat pins); some also accept Type B, which adds an earth pin, but most take only Type A. The UK uses 230 V, 50 Hz and Type G plugs with three rectangular pins. For the laptop charger, check its label: if it says 'INPUT 100-240V, 50/60Hz', as most do, it will work in Japan with just a plug adapter. For the hair dryer: a UK 230 V dryer on a 100 V supply will run slowly and won't heat properly, and a plug adapter does not change the voltage. Use a dual-voltage travel dryer, or a step-up transformer rated for the dryer's power (bulky for a high-wattage dryer), or do without.

UK: 230 V, Type G; adapter needed for the plug shape

Penalize: stating Japan uses 220-240 V or Type G/C sockets, or that a plug adapter alone makes a 230 V-only dryer work properly

question: Explain how the Schengen 90/180-day rule works for a visa-free visitor, with an example.
answer: A visa-exempt visitor may stay in the Schengen Area for at most 90 days in any 180-day period. The limit covers the Schengen Area as a whole, not each country, so days in France, Italy, Germany and the other member states all count toward the same 90. The 180-day window is rolling: on any day of your stay, count back 180 days and add up every day you spent in the Schengen Area; the total must not exceed 90. The day you enter and the day you leave both count as days of stay. Days spent in European countries outside Schengen, such as Ireland, do not count. Example: you spend 60 days in Spain and Italy, leave the area for 30 days, and come back. On your return, the previous 180 days still include those 60 days, so you can stay only about 30 more days before reaching 90; you regain days only as the earlier ones fall out of the 180-day window. Longer stays need a national long-stay visa or a residence permit. The European Commission's short-stay calculator can check your dates.
rubric: 90 days within any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area (not per country)
Rolling window: look back 180 days from each day of stay; entry and exit days count
Days outside Schengen (e.g. Ireland) don't count; long stays need a national visa/permit

question: I'm visiting Venice in November. What is acqua alta, and how should I deal with it?
answer: Acqua alta ('high water') is when exceptionally high tides in the northern Adriatic push the lagoon above the level of Venice's lowest streets and squares, flooding them. It comes from a combination of astronomical tides, the Adriatic's natural sloshing (seiche) and weather, especially the sirocco wind blowing up the Adriatic and low pressure. It happens several times a year at irregular intervals, mostly in the colder months, so November is a typical time, and an episode usually lasts a few hours around high tide. Low areas such as Piazza San Marco flood first. How to deal with it: follow the forecasts, since sirens sound a sequence of tones that increases with the expected tide level, and live tide readings and predictions are posted (for example on a board at the Campanile in Piazza San Marco); wear waterproof boots or use the raised walkways set up during floods; and get an acqua alta map from a tourist office showing higher, dry routes. Since October 2020 the MOSE mobile barriers at the three lagoon inlets (Lido, Malamocco, Chioggia) have been raised for the highest forecast tides, preventing the worst floods, but smaller acqua alta can still wet St Mark's Square. The record is 194 cm in November 1966; the November 2019 flood reached 187 cm.

Season: mostly autumn-winter (November typical); lasts a few hours around high tide
